# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 41 (Bu-Vb Pc41)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc41
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 41
**Title (English, from literature):** Giving food to non-Buddhist monastics
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

**Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 41** (Vin IV 92), entitled *Acelaka*, sets down the disciplinary rule prohibiting a Buddhist monk from personally giving solid food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*) with his own hand (*sahatthā*) to an unclad ascetic (*acelaka*), a male wandering mendicant (*paribbājaka*), or a female wandering mendicant (*paribbājikā*) [Dutt 1924; Hüsken 1997]. Any monk who does so commits an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiya*) [Dutt 1924]. In the introductory narrative, the recipient of the food is specifically described as an Ājīvika, but the legal commentary (*padabhājaniya*) generalizes this to any non-Buddhist sectarian mendicant (*titthiya*), defining a *paribbājaka* as any renunciant other than a Buddhist monk or novice [Dutt 1924; Hüsken 1997]. In her study of Theravāda Vinaya, Ute Hüsken notes that the commentary (*Samantapāsādikā*) extends the rule strictly, considering it an offense even if a monk hands food to his own parents if they have gone forth into an outside religious sect; exemptions (*anāpatti*) apply if the food is not presented directly with one's own hand or if the items transferred do not constitute edible food [Hüsken 1997]. Modern scholars note this rule as a key regulation governing monastics' interactions with rival mendicant traditions [Bechert et al. 1997].

English translations include that of Bhikkhu Brahmali. Curated parallels exist widely across Buddhist traditions, appearing in the Theravāda Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and Parivāra, as well as the Bhikṣu- and Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa and Vibhaṅga texts of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsaṅghika, and Dharmaguptaka lineages preserved in Chinese, Tibetan, and Sanskrit. Machine text-matching via DharmaNexus demonstrates substantial internal reuse with Vinaya Khandhaka treatises (particularly the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, *Mahākhandhaka*, and *Cīvarakkhandhaka*) as well as cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and Jayarakṣita's *Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā* [DharmaNexus].
